title: Pixelasset coat palette (base colour → coat colour)
description: A coat of an ingested third-party family: a colour-for-colour correspondence measured off one named sheet, applied to another coat's geometry. Deliberately NOT palette.schema.json's `coats`, which is a seven-role style ramp (OUTLINE…ACCENT) replacing `roles` wholesale for Path C's role-character templates. These colours have no roles and cannot acquire them — #5e3420 is not SHADOW in any style sense, it is whatever the pack's artist used. Folding them in would also mean re-measuring a third-party PNG bumps palette_v1, versioning the pack inside the §19 style record and changing every Path C asset's palette_version. §23 is satisfied instead by every coat of a family sharing one key space, named in `base` and checked for set equality.

base.description: The coat whose colours are this coat's keys. Every coat of a family declares the same base, and `map`'s key set is checked against it — that shared key space is the thing variants actually share.

source.description: The one sheet this coat was measured from. Pinned to a single sheet on purpose: the pack is not self-consistent across its own sheet families, so a coat that matched all of them cannot exist. Verified at extraction and in the tests, never during a build — see coat.verify_source.

map.description: One row per colour of the base coat's visible palette, ordered by pixel count descending so two coat files diff row for row. A list of rows rather than a YAML mapping because yaml.safe_load silently keeps the last of duplicate keys, which is the exact failure that must be caught; and rather than two parallel lists because those encode the correspondence in line numbers, so a reorder would silently remap the whole coat. Key distinctness is enforced by the loader, not here: JSON Schema 2020-12 has no unique-by-property keyword, and uniqueItems only dedupes whole rows.

from.description: A colour of the base coat. These are the keys and must be pairwise distinct.

to.description: What that colour becomes. Duplicates are legal and intentional: a coat whose art uses fewer colours than the base names the same target twice, which is how black's eleven colours cover bay's thirteen steps.
